title: Head injuries: first aid and watching for deterioration
intro: A blow to the head can affect the brain even without an obvious wound or loss of consciousness. Concussion may cause headache, dizziness, memory problems or difficulty concentrating. Appearance alone cannot establish severity. First aid protects breathing and prevents further injury while arranging the right assessment.

sections.heading: Make the scene safe and check breathing
paragraphs: Approach only when safe. Speak to the person and check responsiveness and normal breathing. Call emergency services for an unresponsive person. If breathing is absent or abnormal, follow dispatcher instructions for resuscitation and use an available defibrillator. Possible neck injury must not prevent lifesaving airway care.

sections.heading: Recognize emergency warning signs
paragraphs: Call 112 for difficulty waking, seizures, new weakness, abnormal speech or walking, repeated vomiting, worsening severe headache, fluid from the ears or nose, penetrating wounds or a high-energy accident. Do not drive the injured person yourself if unstable. Symptoms can develop after an initially reassuring period.

sections.heading: Protect the person while help arrives
paragraphs: Avoid unnecessary movement and support the head and neck without forcing a position. Do not remove embedded objects or press directly on a suspected skull fracture. Monitor breathing continuously. If unconscious but breathing normally, airway protection takes priority; follow dispatcher guidance on turning safely. Stay nearby and keep the person warm.

sections.heading: Explain risks to the assessing service
paragraphs: Report the mechanism, time, blackout, memory gaps, vomiting and changes you witnessed. Mention blood thinners, bleeding disorders, previous brain surgery, alcohol or drugs. A person taking blood thinners needs prompt advice even if initially well. Infants and people who cannot describe symptoms need particular attention. Do not assume confusion is simply intoxication.

sections.heading: Follow observation and recovery instructions
paragraphs: Home care is appropriate only after suitable advice or assessment. A responsible adult should observe the person for at least 24 hours. Sleep is allowed, but difficulty waking is an emergency. Avoid alcohol, sedatives unless prescribed for this situation and activities risking another impact. Follow an individual return-to-school, work, driving and sport plan; seek review for persistent or worsening symptoms.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: symptoms after a match
examples.text: Luka is briefly confused after a collision. He stops playing and receives assessment rather than returning because he did not faint. His companion reports the confusion and watches for deterioration.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: medicines change the decision
examples.text: Ana bumps her head and feels well but takes an anticoagulant. She contacts a medical service promptly and reports the medicine rather than deciding a small bruise makes assessment unnecessary.

questions: Does the injury mechanism or my medicine require urgent assessment?
